pages.text:
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE, Plaintiff, v. KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6, Defendants. ____________________________________/ | Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION UNDER RULE 26(d)(1) FOR PRESENT AUTHORIZATION TO SERVE ONE INTERROGATORY ON NCMEC CONCERNING PLAINTIFF’S FULL LEGAL NAME

I.	INTRODUCTION

“If you deserve the hammer, you’re getting the hammer.” Here, in Ballentine v. Hall, et al., there is a man who either deserves the hammer or a man who deserves the right to clear his name.

There are either CyberTipline reports that connect Marvelle J. Ballentine to the most vile type of human conduct imaginable, or there are not.

Should documents exist that connect Marvelle J. Ballentine to the most heinous type of conduct a human being can engage in, and should those documents establish that he committed such conduct, then Marvelle J. Ballentine should get the hammer. It should include, if warranted by law, permanent separation from society, as well as prompt and immediate dismissal of this action.

If no such report exists, then Marvelle J. Ballentine deserves to vindicate his name and begin the process of reintegration into his personal and professional networks.

The road has been long. The answer has been pursued in courts from the East Coast to the West Coast. The pursuit of that answer has been met with fierce resistance from both the defense and the Courts. Such resistance may be counterproductive to the interests of child safety if, in fact, Mr. Ballentine is a predator. Outing him as such would allow NCMEC to immediately place the evidence in the hands of law enforcement and begin the process of delivering the hammer to Mr. Ballentine. If the defense is unable to supply the report, then substitute the pen for the hammer.

The pen should say: “The motion is granted.”

II.	EITHER POSSIBILITY FAVORS AN ANSWER

Assume the worst. Assume that Marvelle J. Ballentine committed crimes against children and that the reports contain evidence of it. Children deserve protection. He deserves accountability. Now assume that the association is baseless. Then he has a name to clear. Either possibility favors getting the facts right. The man asking for those facts is Marvelle J. Ballentine.

NCMEC says it received two reports. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. Yet it “takes no position” on Plaintiff’s denial of reportable conduct, “as it cannot know whether or not that is true.” ECF No. 11 at 9. It “took no position as the validity of the reports.” Id. at 10. Plaintiff has received no correspondence from NCMEC indicating a law-enforcement referral and no law-enforcement contact concerning the matters addressed in the April 22 letters. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 20. He has the letters. He lives with the association. He is still asking for the facts.

NCMEC’s positions, in its own words:

Position | Source

“NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.” | April 22, 2026 letters, ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3

“The Statements are True, and Thus Not Actionable.” | ECF No. 11 at 8

“NCMEC takes no position on that allegation, as it cannot know whether or not that is true.” | ECF No. 11 at 9

“NCMEC took no position as the validity of the reports, or expressed anything relating to the conduct that lead to the reports.” | ECF No. 11 at 10

“He cannot plausibly assert that is the case, because he does not have access to those reports.” | ECF No. 11 at 9

“Plaintiff simply cannot possibly know what CyberTipline Reports have been received by NCMEC.” | ECF No. 33 at 3

NCMEC “has reason to be concerned that information provided in discovery in this matter could give rise to further litigation from Mr. Ballentine.” | No. 1:26-cv-01341, ECF No. 11 at 4

“NCMEC respectfully requests that dismissal be with prejudice, and Plaintiff not be granted leave to amend.” | ECF No. 11 at 17

NCMEC asserts receipt. NCMEC asserts truth. NCMEC does not know whether the conduct occurred. NCMEC does not vouch for the validity of the reports. NCMEC holds the only copies. NCMEC’s stated concern about discovery is further litigation. NCMEC asks that this action end now, with prejudice, on the truth of the letters.

The letters contain no limiting language. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3; FAC ¶¶ 190, 211. The limiting language exists. NCMEC wrote it. NCMEC placed it in a memorandum filed August 12, 2026, not in the letters. ECF No. 11 at 9–10.

NCMEC’s truth argument rests on Dangerfield v. WAVY Broadcasting, Inc., 228 F. Supp. 3d 696 (E.D. Va. 2017). ECF No. 11 at 10. The broadcast in Dangerfield stated that the plaintiff was “accused of rape.” 228 F. Supp. 3d at 702. The accusation existed. The analogy NCMEC chose holds if a report naming “Marvelle J. Ballentine” exists. NCMEC has not said whether one does. Exhibit A asks.

If NCMEC answers “Yes,” it holds a report, received between July 1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, that contained the name “Marvelle J. Ballentine” as originally received. The statute directs NCMEC to “make available each report” to law enforcement. 18 U.S.C. § 2258A(c). A sworn “Yes” discloses to Plaintiff nothing that the statute has not already placed within reach of a federal agency. On that answer, Plaintiff has the fact he has sought since April 9, 2026.

If NCMEC answers “No,” it holds no such report. The letters placed “Marvelle J. Ballentine” first in a sentence about two CyberTipline reports, on NCMEC letterhead, over the signature of its Corporate Counsel. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. On that answer the statement is false as to the person the letters were addressed to. The remedy lies in this Court.

If NCMEC answers “Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry,” it has stated its present knowledge under oath. Its truth defense then proceeds on a sworn position.

No answer discloses a report’s contents, a submitter, a third party, or an image. No answer requires production. No answer harms a child. The one interest that delay serves is the interest NCMEC named in July 2026: further litigation from Mr. Ballentine. No. 1:26-cv-01341, ECF No. 11 at 4. Rule 26(d)(1) does not list that interest.

NCMEC is the clearinghouse. It receives reports. It does not investigate them. It does not adjudicate them. “Cannot know” whether conduct occurred is consistent with that role. What names a report contains is not a matter NCMEC cannot know. It is the one fact in NCMEC’s filings that NCMEC has never disclaimed. It is the only fact Exhibit A asks for. Each answer places this action in a defined posture. The Court cannot assess that posture without the answer. The answer is one word.

III.	THE QUESTION ASKED AND THE LETTERS RECEIVED

On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted to NCMEC’s Legal Department an “Advance Notice of Intended Subpoenas” identifying Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 6:26-cv-00376-AGM-DCI (M.D. Fla.) (the “376 Action”), and Ballentine v. Anderson, No. 6:26-cv-00286-AGM-DCI (M.D. Fla.) (the “286 Action”). ECF No. 7-6 at 2. The notice stated that each draft subpoena “will be formally served after the notice period has run.” Id. It stated the question both subpoenas asked: “whether a CyberTipline report under 18 U.S.C. § 2258A was filed concerning the Facebook account associated with Marvelle J. Ballentine and terminated on or about July 4, 2022.” Id. at 2–3. Schedule A requested “a document sufficient to show whether” NCMEC “received or maintains any CyberTipline report, referral, or submission concerning” three listed identifiers and, if none existed, “a written statement so stating after a reasonable search.” Id. at 5, 8. No subpoena was served. FAC ¶¶ 57, 72.

On April 22, 2026, Hall signed two letters on NCMEC letterhead, one keyed to each action. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. Each letter opened: “In response to your subpoena issued April 9, 2026.” Id. Each letter then stated: “NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.” Id. The letters did not produce the document Schedule A described. FAC ¶ 77. The three identifiers were quoted from Plaintiff’s own April 9 notice. FAC ¶ 78. The letters identified no report number, report date, or reporting provider. FAC ¶ 91. They linked the identifiers with “and/or” without stating that any single identifier corresponded to either report. FAC ¶ 93. They did not state whether any identifier appeared in any report or in any provider submission. FAC ¶ 96. They did not state that NCMEC had determined that the three identifiers referred to one person. FAC ¶ 97.

The requested discovery now concerns one identifier. Exhibit A asks whether any report NCMEC holds, received from any reporting party between July 1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, inclusive, contained the full legal name “Marvelle J. Ballentine” as originally received. The letters’ sentence does not state whether that name appears in any original report. That question remains unanswered.

IV.	NCMEC HAS DEFENDED THE LETTERS WITHOUT SUPPLYING THE REQUESTED ANSWER

NCMEC describes the letters as precise compliance. It states that “NCMEC responded precisely as requested, mirroring the language utilized by Plaintiff in the Schedules accompanying the subpoenas.” ECF No. 11 at 3. It states that NCMEC “responded, without waiting for formal service, in precisely the manner instructed, and using precisely the language instructed.” Id. at 16.

NCMEC argues truth and access together. It states that Plaintiff “cannot plausibly assert” falsity “because he does not have access to those reports,” and that a person would be upset to learn “that they, or a person with the same name, or their e-mail address—is linked with a report to NCMEC.” Id. at 9. It states that it “did not add any narrative or context.” Id. at 11. It states that “Plaintiff simply cannot possibly know what CyberTipline Reports have been received by NCMEC.” ECF No. 33 at 3. It repeats the access argument in opposing amendment. ECF No. 74 at 5.

Hall “adopts and joins in” those arguments. ECF No. 45 at 1.

None of those statements answers the question Exhibit A asks. NCMEC states that two reports were received for identifiers Plaintiff listed. NCMEC does not state whether any report, as originally received, contained “Marvelle J. Ballentine.” NCMEC’s own memorandum preserves three referents: Plaintiff, “a person with the same name,” or an email address. ECF No. 11 at 9. NCMEC also states that it “takes no position” on whether Plaintiff engaged in conduct violating a statute enumerated in 18 U.S.C. § 2258A, “as it cannot know whether or not that is true.” Id. That statement concerns misconduct. It is not a statement that NCMEC does not know whether it received reports or what its reports contain. Receipt of a report and proof of wrongdoing are different questions.

Plaintiff asked the question directly. On August 13, 2026, Plaintiff asked counsel for NCMEC and Hall whether either report, as received from the reporting provider, contained his full legal name, the name “Jay Ballentine,” or the email identifier. ECF No. 20 at 1–2; ECF No. 26-1 ¶¶ 14–15; Ballentine Decl. ¶ 7. Counsel wrote that “you got exactly what you asked for, using the language you provided.” ECF No. 26-1 ¶ 16; Ballentine Decl. ¶ 7. That response did not answer whether the full name appeared in an original report. As of November 7, 2026, no defendant or counsel had supplied the sworn original-report answer requested here. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 6. [If the November 9, 2026 conference produced a refusal to answer voluntarily, insert: “On November 9, 2026, counsel declined to provide the original-report answer voluntarily. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 18.” If counsel stated a different position, state it as stated.] An answer of “Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry” states present knowledge.

V.	PLAINTIFF HAS SWORN TO HIS OWN ACCOUNT PRACTICES

Plaintiff has twice sworn that, before April 22, 2026, he never used “Marvelle J. Ballentine” to create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any Meta account; that he used “Jay Ballentine”; and that his full legal name appeared in the April 9 materials because it is his legal name and the name under which the Florida actions were pending. ECF No. 31 ¶¶ 3–8; ECF No. 59-2 ¶¶ 3–10; Ballentine Decl. ¶ 3. Those facts explain the inquiry. NCMEC’s records answer whether the full name appears in an original report.

VI.	PRESENT PROCEDURAL POSTURE

In the earlier action, Ballentine v. National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, No. 1:26-cv-01341-MSN-WBP (E.D. Va.) (the “1341 Action”), Plaintiff’s July 16, 2026 opposition reported that no party discovery had been served and that on July 13, 2026 Plaintiff had transmitted a Rule 26(f) planning proposal. No. 1:26-cv-01341, ECF No. 13 at 2–3. On July 15, 2026, Hall and NCMEC moved to stay pre-answer discovery and the parties’ Rule 26 obligations until the pending motion to dismiss was decided. Id., ECF No. 11 at 1, 3–4. On July 17, 2026, the Court granted the motion and stayed discovery pending resolution of the motion to dismiss. Id., ECF No. 15 at 1. The order states no reasons. Id.

In this action, NCMEC stated that if Plaintiff sought a Rule 26(f) conference before the Court ruled on its motion to dismiss, “NCMEC would move to stay that requirement pending resolution.” ECF No. 33 at 3. No separately docketed defense motion seeking that stay appears through the November 5, 2026 entry. On October 7, 2026, Magistrate Judge Davis denied Plaintiff’s earlier limited-discovery motions “as premature” because “currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case.” ECF No. 84 at 1–2. On October 29, 2026, Magistrate Judge Fitzpatrick denied Plaintiff’s scheduling and planning motions, stating that “the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2. Those two orders define the present posture. NCMEC’s October 28, 2026 response to Plaintiff’s planning request again described a conference as premature while dispositive motions remained pending. ECF No. 107-3 at 3; see ECF No. 119 at 4–5. Plaintiff therefore seeks the court-order exception directly.

On November 5, 2026, the Court terminated the December 16, 2026 setting entered on November 3 and directed that the motions then set be decided on the papers. Plaintiff independently waives argument on this application. Three motions to dismiss are pending. ECF Nos. 10, 21, 45. NCMEC seeks dismissal with prejudice. ECF No. 11 at 17. Plaintiff’s objections to ECF No. 84 and his requests concerning ECF Nos. 96 and 108 are pending at ECF Nos. 89, 93, 109–113, and 118–123. This Motion does not require their resolution. The pending dismissal requests make clarification of the existing injury urgent while ordinary discovery remains deferred. Authorization does not depend on showing that a Rule 12 ruling requires additional evidence.

VII.	ARGUMENT

A.	Rule 26(d)(1) authorizes the requested order

Rule 26(d)(1) provides: “A party may not seek discovery from any source before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f), except in a proceeding exempted from initial disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1)(B), or when authorized by these rules, by stipulation, or by court order.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1); see ECF No. 33 at 3 (quoting the rule). The court-order exception is part of the rule. A scheduling order is not a textual prerequisite to that authority. “Courts may allow discovery to begin before a Rule 26(f) conference occurs.” Gallagher, ECF No. 70 at 17. “[A] court can order expedited discovery.” Novoluto, ECF No. 44 at 3. “District courts enjoy broad discretion to supervise discovery.” Gallagher, ECF No. 70 at 17. The exercise of that authority is discretionary.

Plaintiff asks for an express, limited exception to the posture described in ECF No. 108. The exception must be ordered. Plaintiff asks the Court to order it for Exhibit A alone.

B.	The Court should apply the modified preliminary-injunction test

The Federal Rules “do not specify a standard for assessing when to grant Motions for Expedited Discovery, and the Fourth Circuit has not established one.” Gallagher, ECF No. 70 at 17 (quoting Does v. Musk, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 100405, at *8 (D. Md. May 27, 2025)). Courts in this District “apply a modified preliminary injunction test” to such requests. Id. (quoting Kia Motors Am., Inc. v. Greenbrier GMC, Inc., 2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 252505, at *12 (E.D. Va. Dec. 11, 2020)). That test “looks to whether the Plaintiff has made a strong showing of merits and irreparable harm to Plaintiff in the absence of expedited discovery and is justified by the idea that granting court relief outside of the federal rules should be limited to unusual circumstances.” Id. at 17–18 (quoting Kia Motors, 2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 252505, at *12–13). Novoluto states the same test: “a strong showing of success on the merits of the action as well as a showing that irreparable harm is likely in the absence of expedited discovery,” premised on “the idea that granting court relief outside of the federal rules should be limited to unusual circumstances.” Novoluto, ECF No. 44 at 3–4.

Plaintiff asks the Court to apply that test. It is the framework these decisions apply, not a categorical rule the Fourth Circuit has prescribed for every early-discovery request. Part VII.G separately shows good cause under the additional approach this District has used for limited identifying discovery. The application below is organized as merits, irreparable harm, and unusual circumstances with tailoring.

The merits assessment requested here is preliminary and concerns this discovery application. Plaintiff seeks no final adjudication of liability in the authorization order. Novoluto assessed the merits on a “preliminary review of materials furnished by both parties.” ECF No. 44 at 4.

C.	The record supports a strong showing on the merits of Counts I, II, and VI

Counts I and II plead defamation per se and, in the alternative, defamation by implication, concerning the 376-Action letter and the 286-Action letter respectively. FAC ¶¶ 182–223. Count VI pleads insulting words under Va. Code § 8.01-45. FAC ¶¶ 252–260. The operative pleading, the letters, Plaintiff’s sworn account practices, and the existing briefing supply the following showing.

Publication. The FAC alleges that Hall directed each letter to a commercial mail-receiving agency address. It alleges that an agency employee opened, reviewed, scanned, and uploaded each letter on or about April 28, 2026. It alleges that the account administrator later opened and read both letters. FAC ¶¶ 103–114, 184–186, 205–207. The letters supply the words. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3.

Of and concerning Plaintiff. Each letter is addressed to Marvelle J. Ballentine, lists “Marvelle J. Ballentine” first, and carries the caption of an action in which Plaintiff is the plaintiff. ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3; FAC ¶¶ 187, 208. The full name placed first and the separate case captions support the pleaded person-level meaning. The letters do not state which person or identifier any original report identifies.

Defamatory meaning and implication. The FAC alleges that a reasonable reader would understand the association of Plaintiff’s full legal name with two CyberTipline reports, on NCMEC letterhead and over the signature of its Corporate Counsel, to convey that NCMEC had received reports linking Plaintiff personally to suspected child-exploitation conduct that could be available to law enforcement. FAC ¶¶ 188–190, 209–211. The letters contain no limiting language. Id. ¶¶ 190, 211. NCMEC itself “cannot know” whether the conduct occurred and took “no position” on the reports’ validity. ECF No. 11 at 9–10. A reader of the letters was given neither statement. The claim concerns the meaning these letters conveyed, including by implication.

Falsity. The FAC alleges that the imputation, whether per se or by implication, is false. FAC ¶¶ 191, 212. Plaintiff has sworn that he never used the full legal name on any Meta account. ECF No. 31 ¶¶ 3–8; ECF No. 59-2 ¶¶ 3–10. The letters repeated the names Plaintiff supplied without identifying whether the legal name was in an original report. FAC ¶¶ 77–78, 91–97. That combined record supports an inference that the person-level association is false. The alleged literal falsity of a person-level statement is distinct from the asserted implication of reported child-exploitation conduct.

Fault and intended implication. The FAC pleads negligence in issuing the letters without verifying the asserted subpoena, and actual malice as to the implication from the selection of wording, the disjunctive linkage, and the absence of disambiguation. FAC ¶¶ 192–194, 213–215. It pleads the notice and timing: advance notice on April 9; issuance thirteen days into the announced notice period; one day after the April 21 motions directed at the same discovery; before any served subpoena; with report metadata omitted. Id. ¶¶ 55–78, 91–97. The combined circumstances support the asserted inference.

Injury. The FAC pleads presumed damages under the per se theory and actual damages. FAC ¶¶ 197–202, 218–223. The letters led Plaintiff to seriously contemplate his continued participation in the Florida proceedings. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 4. The present effects are sworn at Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 8–16. Part VII.D develops the separate likely-irreparable-harm showing.

Insulting words. Section 8.01-45 makes actionable words that, from their usual construction and common acceptation, are construed as insults and tend to violence and breach of the peace. The FAC pleads that the words of each letter, in the context pleaded, are such words. FAC ¶¶ 252–260. The inquiry is the ordinary meaning and context of these words, not a prediction of violence by Plaintiff.

The asserted defenses do not eliminate the requested preliminary showing.

Truth. NCMEC argues that the letters are true and that Plaintiff cannot plead otherwise because he lacks access to the reports. ECF No. 11 at 9; ECF No. 74 at 5. NCMEC also states that it “cannot know” whether Plaintiff engaged in reportable conduct and that it “took no position as the validity of the reports.” ECF No. 11 at 9–10. NCMEC vouches for its words. NCMEC withholds the records that would test them. NCMEC disclaims the meaning a reader would take from them. The disclaimer concedes what the implication claim alleges: the letters convey more than NCMEC knows. A record responsive to one listed term is not the pleaded person-level imputation. ECF No. 20 at 6. NCMEC’s position that the letters accurately describe reports does not state whether the full legal name was in an original report. Exhibit A asks the one fact NCMEC does know.

Litigation privilege. NCMEC relies on the letters’ connection to litigation and on the proposition that a recipient may respond to a subpoena without service. ECF No. 11 at 5–7. Virginia’s absolute privilege can reach qualifying communications outside the courtroom, including communications preliminary to a proposed judicial proceeding that relate to a proceeding contemplated in good faith and under serious consideration and are disclosed only to interested persons. Mansfield v. Bernabei, 284 Va. 116, 122, 124–25, 727 S.E.2d 69 (2012); ECF No. 20 at 4–5. The FAC alleges advance notice of an intended subpoena, no served process, no court order, no requested early answer, letters sent to Plaintiff alone and filed with no tribunal, and an asserted purpose to deter Plaintiff’s participation and testimony. FAC ¶¶ 70–80, 158–162. The letters are keyed to existing cases, and the pleaded function and audience of these letters distinguish them from a communication made in or preliminary to a judicial proceeding. On the pleaded facts the predicate for the privilege is not established.

Section 2258D. Section 2258D(a) bars civil claims against NCMEC and its personnel “arising from the performance of the CyberTipline responsibilities or functions of NCMEC,” as described in that section, § 2258A, § 2258C, or § 404 of the Missing Children’s Assistance Act, or from NCMEC’s efforts to identify child victims. 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a); ECF No. 11 at 7. Subsection (b) withdraws that protection for intentional misconduct, actual malice, reckless disregard of a substantial risk of causing injury without legal justification, or a purpose unrelated to those functions. 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(b). Subsection (c) separately excludes ordinary business activity. Id. § 2258D(c); ECF No. 20 at 5. The FAC pleads that neither letter was a report, referral, or disclosure under §§ 2258A–2258C and that each was voluntary legal correspondence issued without any served subpoena or court order. FAC ¶ 80. In the alternative it pleads intentional conduct, actual malice, reckless disregard, and an unrelated purpose, with the facts from which those states of mind are inferred. Id. ¶¶ 80, 192–194, 213–215. The classification of the correspondence is a pleaded fact question. The pleaded facts tie the subsection (b) exceptions to Hall’s selection of wording and timing rather than to a label.

Section 20505. Section 20505(a) bars damages liability for defamation, libel, slander, or harm to reputation arising out of an action or communication “in connection with any clearinghouse, hotline, or complaint intake or forwarding program.” 34 U.S.C. § 20505(a); ECF No. 11 at 7. Its exceptions are actual malice and a purpose unrelated to an activity mandated by federal law. 34 U.S.C. § 20505(b); ECF No. 20 at 6. It contains no ordinary-business exception and no separate reckless-disregard exception. The FAC pleads actual malice from the invocation of an unserved subpoena and the selection of wording associating Plaintiff personally with reports he had supplied by name, and it pleads a purpose unrelated to any mandated activity: deterring Plaintiff’s attendance and testimony in the two federal actions. FAC ¶¶ 80, 158, 162, 194, 215. The pleaded purpose and knowing personal association supply Plaintiff’s argued application.

Access and pleading. NCMEC objects that Plaintiff cannot plead falsity because he lacks access to the reports. ECF No. 74 at 5. The Fourth Circuit permits supported allegations on information and belief, has rejected a rationale confining that practice to information exclusively within a defendant’s control, and has recognized that plaintiffs cannot always supply evidentiary support before discovery. Lowy v. Daniel Defense, LLC, 167 F.4th 175, 199 (4th Cir. 2026) (majority opinion; slip op. at 33–35). That principle answers the access objection.

The letters, Plaintiff’s sworn naming facts, the pleaded context, and the responses to the actual defenses support the strong showing Part VII.B requires. The one answer sought would resolve the defined original-name uncertainty on which NCMEC’s truth argument rests. Novoluto assessed the merits on claim-specific materials before full discovery. ECF No. 44 at 4.

D.	The unresolved association causes continuing harm

1.	The injury already exists. The association between Plaintiff’s full legal name and two CyberTipline reports is already in the public litigation record. The letters use the listed names and email with “and/or.” ECF No. 7-5 at 2–3. Hall and NCMEC attached the letters to their June 16, 2026 dismissal memorandum in the 1341 Action. ECF No. 7-2 at 2, 14, 16. Plaintiff later reproduced the letters here. ECF No. 7-1 ¶¶ 2, 5; ECF No. 7-5. NCMEC defends the letters as accurate. ECF No. 11 at 9; ECF No. 74 at 5.

Plaintiff has never seen a CyberTipline report. He does not know whether any original report contains his full legal name. Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 5–6. The public assertion remains while its original-report identification remains unknown to him. Plaintiff cites the filing history to explain present exposure and uncertainty. Consistent with FAC ¶ 26, he predicates no new claim on a court filing.

Plaintiff previously experienced a refusal of legal services that he understood to be attributable at least partly to his account’s child-sexual-exploitation designation. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 8. His September 2025 complaint recorded the representation obstacle before the letters existed. Id. ¶ 9 & Ex. 1; Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 3:25-cv-07671, ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 11–12 at 3 (N.D. Cal.). The experience explains the present concern.

2.	The injury has continuing consequences. Plaintiff intends to retain counsel for his pending litigation so that he can devote more attention to Docket Entry and his family. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 10. The earlier refusal makes him reluctant to risk another rejection while the association remains unresolved. The letters’ presence in the public record, NCMEC’s defense of them, and Meta’s description of them as the requested discovery add to that concern. Id. ¶ 11. This is a present effect on seeking representation.

Plaintiff is actively developing Docket Entry, an AI-assisted litigation technology business, including its technology, litigation workflows, and professional and operational foundation. Id. ¶ 12. The unresolved association restricts his willingness to participate openly in networking, business development, incubators, accelerators, and founder fellowships. Id. ¶¶ 13–14. The described injury is that current restriction on participation.

The continuing uncertainty causes stress affecting Plaintiff’s daily work, family responsibilities, and intended transition away from handling the litigation personally. Id. ¶ 15. The declaration supplies these present consequences. FAC ¶¶ 169–180 separately describe the earlier effects, including contemplated withdrawal and the later course of his distress.

3.	Withholding the answer perpetuates the uncertainty. The requested original-name fact bears on the challenged person-level association and NCMEC’s truth defense to Counts I, II, and VI. It can test and narrow a defined factual component of the existing claims while clarifying the same association that continues to affect Plaintiff. FAC ¶¶ 77–78, 91–101, 184–223, 252–260; ECF No. 11 at 9.

NCMEC controls the records needed to answer whether it holds a qualifying report that contained Plaintiff’s full legal name as originally received. The question covers reports received from any reporting party during the defined period. NCMEC has acknowledged that Plaintiff cannot inspect the CyberTipline system. ECF No. 33 at 3. Its earlier response to Plaintiff’s inquiry did not identify whether the full name appeared in an original report. Ballentine Decl. ¶¶ 5–7.

Plaintiff explains that accurate sworn reporting information would inform his decisions about seeking counsel and participating professionally. Ballentine Decl. ¶ 16. NCMEC’s answer would replace an unanswered defined question with the organization’s position after reasonable inquiry. The practical benefit is timely clarification for those present decisions.

A “No” answer would establish NCMEC’s sworn position that it holds no report meeting the defined receipt-period and original-full-name limits. A “Yes” answer would establish its affirmative position within those limits. An “Unable to determine after reasonable inquiry” answer would establish its present knowledge. Each permitted answer states the respondent’s position within the question’s limits.

4.	The procedural posture adds urgency to clarification. NCMEC seeks dismissal with prejudice and advances the truth of its letters. ECF No. 11 at 9, 17; ECF No. 74 at 5. ECF No. 108 at 2 describes the deferral of ordinary discovery until the dismissal motions are resolved. That sequence risks ending ordinary discovery in this action before Plaintiff receives the requested answer. The described consequences continue during that interval.

The existing injury supplies the harm. The pending adjudication adds urgency. A dismissal on an independent legal defense would not establish the letters’ truth or resolve the identification question. This application does not depend on showing that the dismissal motions require additional evidence. It seeks timely, claim-connected authorization under Rule 26(d)(1).

5.	No equivalent remedy supplies the answer now. Preservation keeps records intact but does not disclose the requested information. G.	Good cause independently supports this limited authorization

Courts in this District have also authorized limited identifying discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference on a showing of “good cause.” Strike 3 Holdings, LLC v. Doe, No. 1:25-cv-01308-MSN-WBP, ECF No. 7 at 1–2 (E.D. Va. Aug. 21, 2025). Strike 3 applied a five-factor test: “(1) a concrete showing of a prima facie claim of actionable harm; (2) specificity of the discovery request; (3) the absence of alternative means to obtain the subpoenaed information; (4) a central need for the subpoenaed information; and (5) the party’s expectation of privacy.” Id. at 2 (quoting Strike 3 Holdings, LLC v. Doe, No. 3:23-cv-0546-MOC-SCR, 2023 WL 8720700, at *1 (W.D.N.C. Dec. 18, 2023)). Strike 3 concerned an ex parte request to subpoena an internet service provider for the name and address of an unknown copyright defendant so that the complaint could be served. Id. at 1–3. Plaintiff relies on its identifying-information reasoning with that context disclosed.

ForceX, Inc. v. Technology Fusion, LLC, No. 4:11-cv-88, 2011 WL 2560110, at 5 (E.D. Va. June 27, 2011), applied the modified preliminary-injunction approach and treated relief outside the ordinary rules as limited to unusual circumstances. See Novoluto, ECF No. 44 at 3–4 (citing ForceX*). Plaintiff has developed that framework in full above and independently asks the Court to exercise its Rule 26(d)(1) discretion on the following good-cause grounds.

Concrete claim and central need. Part VII.C supplies the claim-specific showing and Part VII.F the relevance. The answer tests the original-name component of the alleged defamatory association and NCMEC’s truth position. The discovery supports existing claims and their current consequences. The claim connection, not personal reassurance, is the entitlement asserted.

Specificity and burden. Exhibit A states one question, one name, one inclusive window, and three permitted answers with a qualification confined to accuracy. The original-record definitions are fixed. Part VII.F addresses the search universe and carries the respondent-specific detail from the conferral record.

Alternatives and timing. Plaintiff’s own naming knowledge, the letters, the public filings, and preservation do not supply the original reporting fact. The access sequence in Part VI leaves ordinary discovery deferred. The current decisions and effects in Part VII.D explain the need for an answer now.

Privacy. Reporting information is sensitive. Exhibit A discloses no narrative, images, metadata, submitter identity, or other report contents beyond the defined affirmative, negative, or undetermined proposition.

The established claim connection, the present need, the absence of an equivalent answer, the limited disclosure, and the accommodation of any demonstrated response burden supply good cause. This is an additional ground for the same relief.

VIII.	OBTAINING THE ANSWER AND USING IT ARE SEPARATE QUESTIONS

The relief sought is authorization under Rule 26(d)(1), and the Declaration is evidence for this application under Rule 43(c) and 28 U.S.C. § 1746. Goines v. Any later use of outside matters on the dismissal motions is governed by Rule 12(d); neither this Declaration nor discovery authorization automatically amends the FAC or converts those motions.
